info.title: kaas-ui
info.description: A read-only, multi-cluster Kafka UI. Every data route is a GET; there is no mutating endpoint in this document because there is none in the router.

get.description:
The fleet: one section per environment, each holding its clusters, the
schema registries beside them and whatever inventory was configured there.

Sectioned here rather than in the browser because the order is
configuration. Environments come in declared order, and no client can
recover "dev, staging, prod" from three strings that sort the other way. An
environment nothing visible lives in is absent from the response, so a
heading never reports the existence of a cluster the caller may not see —
which is also what makes every URL beneath it unprobeable.

One card per cluster **declared in this environment**, reachable or not.

Scoped to the environment that names it, and that is not decoration: an id
is unique only within its environment, so a listing that reached past this
one could hand a client two clusters called `kafka` with nothing to tell
them apart — and every lookup by id alone would then pick whichever came
first. Absence is a 404 through the same lookup the rest of the namespace
uses, so an environment nobody can see cannot be probed from here either.

**Reads `Cluster::snapshot()` and nothing else**, so it never awaits: the
snapshot sits behind an `ArcSwap` and carries brokers, controller id,
cluster id and every partition's replicas, ISR and offline set. An
unreachable cluster costs a timeout on its own background task, not on this
request — which is the property the dead-cluster fixture exists to prove.

404.description: No such environment, or nothing in it is visible

get.description:
The card, the broker list, and `DescribeCluster` where the cluster answers
it. Where it does not — which is one of the two development clusters today
— the description is absent and the reason travels in `errors`. The page
renders, with a note.

One of the four RPCs that go to a *specific* broker. A broker that is down
yields an error for that node, not for the call — which is why this is
per-node rather than a fan-out that one dead broker can blank.

kaas-lib's version table is **per connection**, deliberately: brokers
mid-rolling-upgrade genuinely disagree, and a cluster-wide table would be
wrong during exactly the window when being right matters. There is no
`cluster.capabilities()` to project from, and fabricating one by using
whichever connection answered gives a UI whose tabs flicker.

So the table is read from an **explicitly named** broker — the lowest node
id unless `?broker=` says otherwise — and `source` says which. The UI
renders that as "as reported by broker 1".

parameters.name: broker
parameters.description: Read the table from this broker

200.description: What this cluster can be asked

get.description:
Four kinds, not one struct with optional fields. `Unrecognized` is a
*successful* description of an undescribable group — it exists, it is
listed, and the UI can say what it is rather than showing a spinner that
never resolves.

Committed offsets joined to the log ends, so lag can be classified rather
than subtracted. "No commit yet", "empty partition", "caught up" and
"behind by n" are four different answers and rendering them all as `0` is
how a lag column becomes something nobody trusts.

parameters.description: Describe these topics instead of listing

get.description:
`describe_topics` prefers `DescribeTopicPartitions` and falls back to
`Metadata` where the newer call is unreachable. Both branches are live
against the two development clusters, and **there is no branch here** —
which is the claim that a partially-implemented broker is indistinguishable
from an old one, made good.

One bounded page, as a plain JSON resource. The same seven modes as the
stream and the same rows — a "load more" button must not produce rows that
differ in shape from the ones already on screen.

parameters.description: Epoch millis, for sinceTime and toTime

parameters.name: filter
parameters.description: Literal substring of the decoded value

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Records to read for this page

get.description:
The seven seek modes, over `text/event-stream`. Events are `messages`,
`progress`, `phase`, `dropped` and `error`; the `id:` on a `messages` event
is `{partition}-{offset}` of its last row.

An `error` event carries the same `ResourceError` shape the rest of the API
uses, so an `UnsupportedApi` arrives with **both** version ranges intact and
the reader can tell "this cluster does not implement it" from "this build
cannot speak it". That distinction is the entire reason the variant carries
two ranges, and flattening it into a message string discards it.

parameters.name: timestamp
parameters.description: Epoch millis, for sinceTime and toTime

parameters.name: filter
parameters.description: Literal substring of the decoded value

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Records to read, ignored by live

get.description:
`TailSpec::limit` is a per-topic target that kaas-lib spreads across
partitions with `div_ceil`, so asking for 20 on a 16-partition topic
genuinely fetches 32. "The last n of a topic" has no single answer across
partitions, so this layer picks one and says so: **the n most recent by
timestamp**, merged across partitions and truncated after the fact.
`total` reports how many were fetched before truncation.

The full payload of one record, fetched when a row is selected and never
before. A record at a given offset never changes, so the frontend caches it
with `staleTime: Infinity` and re-selecting a row costs no request at all.

Implemented with a one-record `scan` rather than the anchored tail the
obvious reading suggests: both land on the right record, but only the scan
carries the **raw bytes of a batch that would not decode**, and a detail
panel that cannot show those is useless for exactly the row that most needs
explaining.

200.description: The record, or the batch that covered it

parameters.name: details
parameters.description: Fetch id, format, version and compatibility

200.description: The subjects of the registry this cluster uses
Every registered version of a subject

get.description:
The identity behind this request and the roles it resolved to.

Deliberately not the place to ask *what may I do here* — that is per
cluster, and it rides on each cluster's card as `grants`. Splitting them
would give the frontend two sources for one answer, and the one it did not
re-fetch would be the stale one.

Answers for anonymous callers too. A deployment with no identity provider
configured has exactly one caller, and saying so plainly is what lets the
frontend render "not signed in" rather than an error.

A GET, like everything else. The document it returns describes an API with
no other verb in it, which the document itself is the easiest way to check.

**Must not consult a cluster.** A liveness probe that fails because
someone's broker is down is a liveness probe that restarts a healthy
process — and with a dozen clusters configured, it restarts it constantly.
This handler touches nothing but the constant below, which is the point.

ClusterCard.description:
One cluster on the fleet dashboard.

Built from `Cluster::snapshot()` and nothing else. The snapshot carries
brokers, controller id, cluster id and every partition's replicas, ISR and
offline set — everything a card renders — and it works on clusters that do
not implement `DescribeCluster`. Enrichment that only some clusters can
answer belongs on the detail page, not on the landing page.

clusterId.description: The broker-reported cluster id, when the snapshot carries one.

controllerId.description: The controller, as the snapshot reports it.

environment.description:
The environment holding it — the first segment of every URL that
reaches it, and half of what identifies it.

grants.description:
What the caller may do here.

Projected per cluster rather than per session because that is what a
role grants: `metadata` on prod and `messages` on dev is one caller
with two answers. The frontend hides what it must not offer — a
messages tab that 403s on click is worse than no tab — which is the
same mechanism the capability projection uses for what a *broker*
cannot do.

`value_type` because the map is keyed by an enum, which utoipa cannot
name on its own — left alone it emits a `$ref` to a schema that does
not exist, and the generated client is broken in a way nothing in Rust
notices.

propertyNames.description:
What a permission is about.

Only what exists. A schema registry and an ACL viewer are Phases 6 and 7,
and their resources arrive with them rather than ahead of them.

id.description: The configured id, unique within that environment.

maxStalenessMs.description:
The staleness ceiling this cluster was configured with, so the UI can
colour the age rather than guessing a threshold.

offlinePartitionCount.description: Partitions with no leader or a replica on a dead broker.

schemaRegistry.description:
The schema registry this cluster references, by its configured id.

`None` is a normal path — a kaas instance beside a Strimzi cluster in
the same environment — and the sidebar reads it to decide whether a
schemas item exists at all, rather than offering one that explains its
own absence.

underReplicatedPartitionCount.description: Partitions whose ISR is smaller than their replica set.

ClusterDetail.description:
The cluster detail page.

The card, plus the two things a detail page adds: the broker list, and
`DescribeCluster` **where the cluster implements it**. Where it does not,
`description` is `None` and the failure travels in the envelope's `errors`
as a named resource — the page renders the snapshot data with a note, not
an error.

Codec.description:
How a payload was read.

The chip in the message list is this value, and the chip is the **override
control**, not a label: auto-detection that cannot be corrected is worse
than none.

Dropped.description:
How many records the server dropped rather than stall the scan.

Silently losing records in a debugging tool is worse than showing a gap,
so this is emitted whenever the count changes and never suppressed.

EnvironmentRegistry.description:
A schema registry inside an environment.

Distinct from the [`ResourceCard`] beside it: that is an inventory line an
operator typed, with its own id and no connection to anything. This one is
the registry that decodes payloads, and it is addressable —
`/api/environments/{env}/schema-registries/{id}`.

It gained that URL when environments did. A registry id is not a global
namespace even so: it is reachable only under an environment the caller can
already see, and only when they can see a cluster there that references it,
which is the same rule `Registry::schema_registry` enforces on the way in.

usedBy.description:
The clusters in this environment that resolve payloads against it.

Rendered as "who uses this", and it is only ever the visible ones —
the list is built from cards this caller already received.

A described group.

Four kinds, not one struct with optional fields. `Unrecognized` is a
**successful** description of an undescribable group: it exists, it is
listed, and the UI can say what it is. Flattening the four into one
all-optional shape moves that knowledge somewhere the compiler cannot
check it.

GroupMember.description: One member of a group, in the shape all three describable kinds share.

assignment.description: The member's assignment, where the protocol reports it decoded.

memberEpoch.description: Member epoch, for the kinds that have one.

subscribedTopics.description: Topics the member subscribed to, where the protocol reports them.

GroupOffset.description: A group's committed offset for one partition, with lag.

committedOffset.description: The committed offset, where there is one.

lag.description: Lag, in its four distinguishable states.

GroupSummary.description: One row of the group list.

describable.description: Whether this group can be described at all.

groupType.description:
Group type. Empty on brokers too old to report one — which is not the
same as unknown, and takes the classic path.

state.description: State, as the broker names it.

oneOf.description: Header value.

auth.description:
`"open"` when no roles are configured, `"enforcing"` when they are.

Here for the same reason the version is: a deployment's security
posture should be answerable from outside the pod. It says nothing a
visitor cannot already tell by loading the page and not being asked to
sign in.

status.description: Always `"ok"` — reaching the handler is the whole check.

version.description:
The running version, so a deployment can be identified without exec'ing
into the pod.

Identity.description:
The caller, for the header and for deciding what to offer them.

Not "what may I do" — that is per cluster and rides on [`ClusterCard`] as
`grants`. This is who the request is from, which the UI needs to render a
"signed in as" line and to know whether signing in is even a thing this
deployment does.

authenticated.description: Whether an identity provider vouched for this caller.

connectors.description:
The named ways to sign in, if this deployment lists any.

Empty is the common case and means "one unlabelled sign-in button" —
the provider is then responsible for asking which connector, which is
what Dex does when it has more than one. A deployment that would rather
ask that question itself, on its own screen, lists them in `auth
.connectors`, and these are what it listed.

Deliberately here rather than on its own endpoint. It is the same
question `login_available` answers — *what should the sign-in control
look like* — and splitting it across two fetches would let the two
halves disagree while one of them was stale.

enforcing.description:
Whether this deployment applies roles at all.

`false` is the open deployment: no identity provider, one anonymous
caller, everything visible. The frontend uses it to decide whether to
offer signing in, and it is worth being explicit about rather than
inferring from an empty role list — which is also what a misconfigured
policy looks like.

loginAvailable.description:
Whether an identity provider is configured at all.

Distinct from `enforcing`, and the frontend needs both: this decides
whether to offer a sign-in button, while `enforcing` decides whether
being signed out means seeing nothing. A deployment can have roles and
no provider — which is a misconfiguration the startup log warns about —
or a provider and no roles, which is an open deployment that happens to
know your name.

roles.description: The roles that covered this caller, in policy order.

subject.description: The stable id. `"anonymous"` when nobody signed in.

oneOf.description: The group has never committed here. Not zero lag — no data at all.
The partition is empty, so there is nothing to be behind.
Committed at the log end.
Behind by a known amount.

The partition's end offset could not be read, so lag is unknown —
which is not the same as zero.

Lag.description: Lag has four states and they must not all render as `0`.

LogDirDto.description: One log directory on one broker.

error.description: The directory's own error, if it has one.

totalBytes.description: Total capacity, where the broker reports it.

LogDirReplicaDto.description: One replica in a log directory.

isFuture.description: Whether this is a future replica being moved in.

offsetLag.description: How far behind the log end this replica is.

LoginConnector.description:
One way to sign in, as the sign-in screen renders it.

The id is opaque and only means something to the provider. Nothing in
kaas-ui interprets it — see [`kaas_ui_auth::Connector`], the configuration
this mirrors.

MalformedDetail.description: A batch that would not decode, with its bytes.

offset.description: The first offset the batch claimed.

raw.description: The raw batch, as hex. The only way to see what is actually on disk.

MalformedRow.description: A batch that would not decode, as a row.

lastOffset.description:
The last offset it claimed, or its own base where the header did not
say — so the row always names a range it can render.

offset.description: The first offset the batch claimed.

Message.description: One record in the message browser.

oneOf.description: The key, rendered.

sizeBytes.description: Size of the value in bytes, before rendering.

timestampType.description: Whether the timestamp is the producer's or the broker's.

transactional.description: Whether the record was written transactionally.

oneOf.description:
The value, rendered. `None` is a tombstone, which is not the same as
an empty value.

allOf.description: The record, with its key, value and headers whole.

oneOf.description: The record, with its key, value and headers whole.

allOf.description: The batch that covered the offset, as hex.

oneOf.description: The batch that covered the offset, as hex.

MessageDetail.description:
The answer to "show me this one record".

Tagged the same way [`StreamRow`] is, and for the same reason: the row a
reader selected might be a batch that would not decode, and the panel that
opens has to be able to say so with the raw bytes rather than showing an
empty record.

MessagePage.description: One page of a window, for "load more".

hasMore.description:
Whether the **read** filled its budget, which is the only honest signal
that there is more.

Not "the page is full": the payload filter runs after the decode, so a
page of three rows may have read five hundred records and have five
hundred thousand still to walk. Deriving this from the row count would
end paging at the first window a selective filter emptied.

items.description: The rows, in the mode's own order.

nextOffset.description:
The anchor to ask for next, or `None` at the end of the window.

One number for every partition, because that is what the seek modes
take: partitions are at different offsets, so this is where to *start*
the next page and not a claim about any particular partition.

oneOf.description:
What a time-mode instant resolved to, and `None` for the other five
modes. See [`resolve`].

NamingStrategy.description: Which of the three formed a subject name.

NoteKind.description:
Why a payload is not what the reader asked for.

Five distinct causes, kept apart because they want five different things
done about them — and because the alternative is a topic that silently
renders as hex with no way to tell a broken registry from a broken URL.

earliestOffset.description: Earliest available offset, on the detail page only.

error.description: The broker's error for this partition, if any.

leader.description: Leader, or `None` when the partition has none.

maxFollowerLag.description:
The worst follower's offset lag, when `?size=true` asked for log dirs.

`None` when sizes were not fetched *and* on a partition with no
followers — a single-copy partition has nobody to lag. `Some(0)` is a
claim: every follower is caught up.

offlineReplicas.description: Replicas on brokers that are down.

replicas.description: The replica set, in assignment order — the placement grid's rows.

replicatedBytes.description:
Every non-future copy of this partition summed, when `?size=true`
asked for it — what the disks hold for this one partition.

The replicated figure rather than the leader's copy, because the
question a per-partition size answers is "which one is the big one",
and because the leader's copy reads `0` on a leaderless partition
rather than declining to answer.

underReplicated.description: ISR smaller than the replica set.

latestOffset.description: The next offset to be written.

records.description: How many records are between them.

Payload.description:
A key or value, rendered with the codec that was used said out loud.

Auto-detection that cannot be seen is worse than none: the reader has to
know whether they are looking at text the producer wrote, at kaas-ui's
guess, or at a schema the registry resolved.

bytes.description: Length in bytes of the original.

oneOf.description: Why this is not what was asked for.
The original bytes, for a codec change with no refetch.
Which schema decoded it, when a registry was involved.

PayloadNote.description: A note attached to a payload, with the sentence to render.

kind.description: What kind of note this is.

RawBytes.description:
The bytes as they arrived, so a codec can be changed without a refetch.

Present exactly when [`Payload::text`] is a *decoded* rendering — Avro,
Protobuf or JSON Schema — because those are the only renderings the
original bytes cannot be recovered from. A hex rendering is already the
bytes, and a UTF-8 one is losslessly convertible to hex in the browser.

hex.description: Lowercase hex of the record as it arrived, framing included.

truncated.description: Whether the hex was cut short.

RegistryCard.description:
One schema registry, as the browser and the fleet render it.

A view of a **registry**, reached through a cluster. Two clusters that
reference `dev` show the same subjects, so the card says which registry is
answering rather than implying the subjects belong to the cluster whose nav
you arrived through.

error.description: What went wrong, where something did.

id.description: The configured id, which is what a cluster's `schema_registry:` names.

status.description: Whether it has been reached, and how it failed if it has not.

url.description:
Where it is. Shown because a registry that is answering the wrong API
is diagnosed by looking at its url.

RegistryStatus.description: The registry health state, flattened for the wire.

ResolvedPartition.description: One partition's answer to a timestamp lookup.

error.description: Why the lookup failed, where it failed rather than answered.

offset.description:
The offset the instant resolved to, or `None` where the broker
reported none.

timestamp.description: The timestamp of the record at that offset, where the broker says.

ResolvedSeek.description:
What an instant actually resolved to, per partition.

Emitted for the two time modes and for no other reason than that a
timestamp seek can be answered correctly and still not land where the
reader expected. `ListOffsets` reports "the first offset at or after this
instant", and a broker with no timestamp index answers **nothing at all** —
a legitimate response that is indistinguishable from "nothing was written
after that time". kaas-ui cannot tell those apart and must not guess; what
it can do is show the answer it got, so an empty window reads as "this
cluster resolved 14:30 to nothing" rather than as a broken seek.

The `kaas` broker in the development environment does exactly this, and
Strimzi does not. See `docs/reference/environment.md`.

timestamp.description: The instant that was asked about, in epoch milliseconds.

unresolved.description:
Whether no partition resolved to an offset.

Precomputed because it is the case worth saying out loud, and a UI that
has to derive it will derive it in three places and differently.

Resource.description:
What a permission is about.

Only what exists. A schema registry and an ACL viewer are Phases 6 and 7,
and their resources arrive with them rather than ahead of them.

ResourceCard.description:
One thing in an environment that is not a Kafka cluster.

**There is no status field, and that is the design.** kaas-ui dials none of
these: it knows a schema registry is configured, not that it is up. A card
carrying `status: "ready"` because a URL was typed correctly would be the
one thing a fleet view must never do — see [`ClusterStatus`], whose
`Connecting` exists so that unknown is not rendered as healthy. The UI says
"not probed" because that is the whole truth kaas-ui has.

Phase 6 connects to the schema registry, and *that* is when this type earns
a health field — one filled in from an attempt, on the one kind that makes
attempts.

endpoint.description: Where it is, when the configuration says.

kind.description: What it is: the icon and the wording, nothing else.

labels.description: Labels, including the `env` its section is keyed by.

code.description: The broker's error code name, when this build has one for it.

codeNumber.description:
The error code's number.

Present even when `code` is null: against a broker newer than the codec
`ErrorCode::Unknown(i16)` is all there is, and the number is the only
searchable thing.

resource.description: Which resource — a topic name, a broker id, a group id.

retriable.description: Whether retrying this one resource is worth offering.

oneOf.description: Both version ranges, when the failure was an unsupported api.

ResourceKind.description:
What a non-cluster resource is.

A closed set on purpose: each variant is an icon and a word in the UI, and
`Other` is the honest home for anything this list has not learned yet
rather than a reason to accept free text that renders as nothing.

SchemaFormat.description: Which of the three registry formats a schema is in.

SchemaRef.description:
Which schema decoded a payload, and which registry answered.

The registry id is here rather than implied by the cluster because a
registry serves an *environment*: two clusters can show the same schema id
and mean the same schema, and a reader has to be able to see that.

format.description: What the registry said the id is.

name.description: The record or message name inside the schema.

registry.description: The registry that answered, by its configured id.

subject.description:
The subject the registry named, where it named one. A schema id can be
registered against more than one subject, so this is "what the registry
returned" rather than an authoritative single answer.

version.description: The version within that subject, where the registry gave one.

SchemaReference.description:
A schema this one refers to, stored separately by the registry.

A resolver that fetches only the id in the payload decodes the simple
topics and fails on the interesting ones — so these are shown, and they are
followed when decoding.

name.description:
The name the referring schema uses — a fully-qualified Avro name, or a
`.proto` import path.

subject.description: The subject the referenced schema is registered against.

SeekMode.description: How a window of a topic was asked for.

StreamPhase.description:
Where a stream is in its life.

A backward window emits `seeking` and nothing else until the whole walk
finishes, because [`kafka_read::tail`] returns a `Vec` — there are no
partial results to show, and a spinner that never changes looks identical
to a hang.

StreamProgress.description: How far a bounded scan has got.

fraction.description:
`0.0`–`1.0`, or `None` before the total is known. A live tail has no
end, so it never has a fraction.

orderingDegraded.description:
Whether the merge is no longer producing a total order across
partitions.

recordsScanned.description: Records read, including those a filter dropped.

reorderWindow.description:
Roughly how many records apart two partitions may be reordered.

Derived from the scan's buffer ceiling spread over the partitions still
running: the merge picks the oldest buffered head, so the window it can
see is what bounds how far out of order the result can be. It is a
caveat to render next to the list, not a promise.

StreamRecord.description: A decoded record, previewed rather than whole.

oneOf.description: The key, cut to [`PREVIEW_CHARS`]. `None` is a keyless record.

timestampType.description: Whether the timestamp is the producer's or the broker's.

transactional.description: Whether the record was written transactionally.

oneOf.description:
The value, cut to [`PREVIEW_CHARS`]. `None` is a **tombstone**, which
is not the same as an empty value — compaction turns on the difference.

allOf.description:
A record that decoded.

Boxed because a decoded payload is much larger than a malformed row —
it carries the schema it resolved against and the bytes it came from —
and a `Vec<StreamRow>` of a thousand rows should not pay a record's
size for every batch that did not decode.

oneOf.description:
A record that decoded.

Boxed because a decoded payload is much larger than a malformed row —
it carries the schema it resolved against and the bytes it came from —
and a `Vec<StreamRow>` of a thousand rows should not pay a record's
size for every batch that did not decode.

allOf.description: A batch that did not. The scan continued past it.

oneOf.description: A batch that did not. The scan continued past it.

StreamRow.description:
One row of the message list, as it crosses an SSE connection.

Two variants, never conflated. A batch that would not decode at the
protocol level is a **row**: kaas-lib's decoder keeps going past it, and
surfacing it is the entire reason that design exists. Folding it into the
stream's `error` event would throw away the one thing the reader needs,
which is *where* in the topic the damage is.

SubjectDetail.description: The versions of one subject, newest last.

compatibility.description: The compatibility mode, where the registry reports one.

errors.description:
Versions the registry listed and would not hand over, with why.

Partial failure is a result: a subject with thirty versions of which
one is unreadable renders twenty-nine and names the thirtieth.

naming.description:
How the subject name was formed, and the topic that recovers from it.

Read from the newest version, because the name a subject is registered
under is a property of the schema in force. A subject whose versions
could not be fetched still gets an answer — the two suffix strategies
need no schema — and `strategy` says which kind of answer it is.

oneOf.description: The registry answering.

subject.description: The subject that was asked for.

versions.description: Every registered version, oldest first, with its text.

SubjectList.description: The subjects one registry holds, and which registry that is.

compatibility.description:
The registry-wide compatibility mode, when `details` was asked for.

What every row without an override of its own is governed by, so the
table can say `BACKWARD` on a registry where nobody has set a
per-subject rule instead of a column of blanks.

dangling.description:
How many matched subjects name a topic that is on no cluster reading
this registry.

A schema outlives the topic it described: deleting a topic does not
touch the registry, so `orders-value` stays registered and stays a
perfectly well-formed name. That is the difference this counts and
`topics` cannot — one is about the *name*, this is about the world.

**Subjects, not topics**: a deleted topic with a key schema and a value
schema is two dangling subjects, which is what a number sitting beside
`subjects` has to mean.

`None` where the question cannot be answered rather than a zero that
would read as "all fine":

* no cluster here references this registry, so there is nothing to
  check against;
* one that does is not connected — its topics are unknown, and calling
  every subject of a cluster that is merely *down* dangling is exactly
  the alarm a fleet view must not raise.

Costs nothing to compute: the topic list is the metadata snapshot each
cluster already holds, so this dials nobody and cannot be slow.

oneOf.description: The registry answering, or `None` where this cluster references none.

subjects.description: The page of subjects, filtered and ordered as asked.

topics.description:
How many distinct topics those subjects name.

Read off the names alone — no registry call and no schema — so this is
`TopicNameStrategy` and nothing else: `{topic}-{record}` needs the
record name to find its seam, and a record-named subject never had a
topic in it. Neither is a failure, and neither is counted here.

Counted over the same set `total` counts, so a `search` narrows them
together. Here rather than in the browser because the alternative was
the fleet card downloading every subject name in the registry in order
to count them — the summary is a property of the whole listing and the
page is not, so `?limit=0` is a legitimate and cheap question.

total.description: How many subjects matched before paging.

recordName.description: The fully-qualified name the schema declares, where it declares one.

topic.description:
The topic the subject names, where the strategy carries one.

`None` under [`NamingStrategy::RecordName`] because there is no topic in
the name, and under [`NamingStrategy::Unrecognized`] because there is no
rule to read it by. The two are not the same fact and `strategy` is what
tells them apart.

SubjectRow.description:
One row of the subject table.

Everything but the name is `Option`, and for one reason: the name is in the
listing the registry already gave us, and the rest is a call per subject.
The client asks for the page first and the columns second.

compatibility.description: The compatibility mode governing this subject.

compatibilityInherited.description:
Whether that mode is the registry's rather than this subject's own.

Two subjects reading `BACKWARD` are not the same fact if one of them
set it and the other is inheriting it — the second changes when the
registry default does.

oneOf.description: Which of the three formats the newest version is.

id.description:
The global schema id of the newest version — the number the wire
format carries.

naming.description:
How the subject name was formed, and the topic that recovers from it.

The same fact [`SubjectDetail`] carries, on every row, because it is
what answers the question from the other end: a *topic* page asks which
subjects name it, and a prefix match cannot tell `orders-value` from
`orders-eu-value`. Free here — `describe` already holds the newest
schema, so the declared name costs no registry call — and without
`details` it is read from the name alone, which still resolves the two
suffix strategies.

SubjectSchema.description: One registered version of a subject.

id.description: The global schema id — the number the wire format carries.

recordName.description:
The fully-qualified name this version declares, where it declares one.

Read once here rather than per request, because the schema cache is
forever and this is a fact about the text. It is what makes the two
record naming strategies readable — see [`crate::naming`].

schema.description:
The schema itself, as the registry stores it. Text rather than parsed,
because this is what Monaco highlights and what a diff is taken over.

subject.description: The subject it is registered against.

brokerIds.description: The brokers holding replicas, for the placement grid's columns.

logDirEntryCount.description:
Log-directory entries holding a copy of this topic.

One per replica per directory, which is what kafbat-ui labels a
"segment count" — `DescribeLogDirs` reports no segment files at all,
so the name is borrowed and wrong. Carried under the name it earns,
and future replicas count: a directory move in flight is an entry on a
disk, whatever the totals above exclude.

logicalBytes.description: Bytes on disk for one copy, when `?size=true` asked for them.

messageCount.description:
Records retained across every partition, when offsets were fetched.

`latest - earliest` summed — and absent, not smaller, when any
partition is missing an end: a sum short one partition is an unmarked
wrong number. The same rule `TopicSummary` applies, in the same place.

offlinePartitionCount.description: Partitions with no leader or an offline replica.

replicatedBytes.description:
Bytes on disk across replicas.

`None` means the caller did not ask, or `DescribeLogDirs` did not
answer for this topic — never that the topic is empty. A zero would be
a claim, and this is the absence of one.

replicationFactor.description:
The smallest replica count across partitions — the same rule, and the
same implementation, as [`TopicSummary::replication_factor`].

Carried here so the overview card does not re-derive it in TypeScript:
the minimum-across-partitions rule is a decision, and a decision that
exists twice in two languages drifts.

TopicPartitions.description: A topic and the partitions of it assigned to a member.

TopicSummary.description: One row of the topic list.

logicalBytes.description: Bytes on disk for one copy, when metrics were asked for.

messageCount.description:
Records retained across every partition, when metrics were asked for.

`latest - earliest` summed, which is what is *retained* rather than
what was ever written — the same distinction the partition table draws.
`None` when the metric was not requested, and also when any one
partition failed to answer: a sum missing a partition is a smaller
number, not a marked one, and nothing in the column would say so.

offlinePartitionCount.description: Partitions with no leader or an offline replica.

replicationFactor.description:
The smallest replica count across partitions, which is what anyone
means by "replication factor".

topicId.description:
The topic uuid, or `None` on a cluster that does not report one.

Absent rather than an empty uuid: a column of zeroes reads as missing
data, and the honest render is no column at all.

UnsupportedApiDetail.description:
The two version ranges an [`Error::UnsupportedApi`] carries.

The pair is a diagnosis rather than a failure, and the three cases render
differently:

* `ours: None` — this build has no schema for the key; bump the codec.
* `broker: None` — the cluster does not implement it at all.
* both present but disjoint — the cluster is behind.

apiKey.description: Its number, which is the searchable thing when the name is unknown.

broker.description: What the broker advertises, as `[min, max]`.

ours.description: What this build speaks, as `[min, max]`.
